newsitem.title: USA: Dollar ends mostly lower in US, mark/yen rebounds.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends mostly lower in US, mark/yen rebounds.

text.p: The dollar ended mostly lower, pressured by a rebound in the mark and by weaker U.S. stock prices ahead of the Federal Reserve's Federal Open Market Committee meeting on Tuesday, traders said.
The dollar finished marginally firmer against the yen, buoyed by the mark's rise against the Japanese currency.
Trading was quiet after a market holiday in Japan and the Yom Kippur holiday thinned market participation in New York.
"It's been a nothing kind of day. Basically people are just waiting for tomorrow's FOMC meeting," said Vincent Amaru, vice president at Citibank.
The dollar ended lower at 1.5125/30 marks but rose to 109.87/97 yen from opening levels of 1.5155/60 and 109.84/89.
The mark rebounded against the yen, ending at 72.66 versus an opening of 72.49, helping to support the dollar against the Japanese currency, traders said.
The dollar initially rose against the mark in early New York trading amid worries over Boris Yeltsin's health after one of his doctors said the Russian president's heart operation may be delayed.
Yeltsin, who has a history of heart problems, is scheduled to undergo heart surgery at the end of this month.
Political uncertainty in Russia hurts the mark because of Germany's close economic ties with Russia.
The dollar later fell from its opening levels, led by declines in U.S. stock prices amid nervousness over interest rates ahead of Tuesday's meeting of Federal Reserve policymakers.

Spooked by the spectre of higher interest rates, the Dow Jones industrial stock average briefly fell more than 50 points in morning trade, giving currency traders an excuse to pare back dollar positions, traders said.
U.S. stocks recovered to end up six points at 5895.
The FOMC meets amid market speculation the central bank is poised to hike short-term interest rates by 0.25 percentage points to put the brakes on inflation.
Traders said it would take a 0.50 percentage point hike in the federal funds rate to move the dollar higher, while a decision to keep interest rates unchanged could push the U.S. unit lower.
"I don't think a 25 basis point hike is tremendously supportive for the dollar in the sense that it's pretty much expected," said Bill Marr, foreign exchange manager at Credit Commerciale de France.
The mark was also well off its overnight lows against its European counterparts.

Overnight, the mark came under selling pressure after European Union finance ministers, meeting in Dublin, Ireland at the weekend, reached agreement on three key areas for bringing European and Montary Union (EMU) closer to fruition.

The ministers agreed to a stability pact to ensure fiscal discipline once EMU begins, a new exchange rate mechanism linking the single European currency to those not participating, and to greater legal certainty for banks in the run-up to monetary union in 1999.
In other trading, the dollar fell to 1.2355/65 Swiss francs compared with 1.2385/95.
It was unchanged against the Canadian dollar at Canadian $1.3665/70.
Sterling climbed to $1.5560/68 from $1.5525/35.
The Australian dollar closed at $0.7917/22.
-- Daniel Rosenblum, 212-859-1662
